claims.text: Experimental melting data for multi-component high-entropy alloys are sparse.
A hybrid framework combining machine-learned interatomic potentials with Einstein-crystal thermodynamic integration can accurately predict melting temperatures of high-entropy alloys.
The hybrid framework can accurately predict entropy of fusion for high-entropy alloys.
Standard empirical potentials fail to capture complex configurational-entropy effects in high-entropy alloys at extreme temperatures.
A machine-learned potential can be trained using a minimal or sparse set of high-temperature DFT calculations.
Standard empirical potentials lack transferability in regimes above 1500 K for alloys containing five or more principal elements.
Standard empirical potentials cannot adequately model the complex electronic environments of high-entropy alloys.
Standard potentials cannot resolve configurational entropy and local atomic-environment fluctuations in high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials can capture the nonlinear dependence of energy on local atomic environments.
Thermodynamic integration using an Einstein-crystal reference provides a rigorous route to absolute free energies.
The calculated free energies enable determination of the solid-liquid coexistence point without empirical melting rules.
The proposed method will predict melting temperatures within 5% of experimental values where such values are available.
The proposed method will produce accurate entropy-of-fusion values for high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method will have significantly lower computational cost than direct ab initio molecular dynamics.
EAM, MEAM, and classical thermodynamic models such as CALPHAD often fail to predict high-entropy-alloy melting points accurately.
The proposed method is valid when sufficient DFT data can be generated to train the machine-learned potential.
The proposed method is valid when the alloy remains a solid solution or a simple intermetallic phase.
The proposed method may fail for systems with strong magnetic ordering or complex phase separation that is absent from the training set.
Prediction accuracy depends strongly on the quality and diversity of the machine-learned potential's training data, and inadequate configurational coverage can make predictions unreliable.
Generating the required DFT training data may be prohibitively expensive when screening very large compositional spaces.
